extracted.intended_audience: people interested in software patent law (patent drafters, practitioners, activists, and the general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Explains the U.S. means-plus-function (functional claiming) doctrine under 35 U.S.C. §112(f), its limits, and its relevance/risks for software patent drafting and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claim per 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: The US Code, Title 35 § 112, says: '(f) Element in Claim for a Combination.— An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim element drafted as a 'means for' performing a function is construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents — not all possible means of performing that function. This statutory text is the controlling rule for how such claim elements are interpreted and limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: coverage only of corresponding structure/material/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent can claim a 'means for' doing something, but this won't cover all means for doing that thing; it will only cover the specific means which is/are described in the rest of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: functional claiming under §112(f) narrows claim scope to what the specification actually discloses as the corresponding structure (and equivalents). Drafters seeking broad coverage via purely functional language risk having the claim confined to disclosed embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose corresponding structure (risk of indefiniteness/invalidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent doesn't describe any means (i.e., no corresponding structure), then the patent can be found invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly held that a patent is invalid as indefinite under Section 112(b) if a claimed 'means' has no particular corresponding structure disclosed in the specification. Reported examples include Function Media, LLC v. Google, Inc., 708 F.3d 1310, 1319 (Fed. Cir. 2013) and Blackboard, Inc. v. Desire2Learn Inc., 574 F.3d 1371, 1382-83 (Fed. Cir. 2009). Anti-pattern: drafting functional claims without describing the algorithms, structures, or acts that implement the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and risk of means-plus-function drafting in software patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters sometimes write software patents with claims to means of doing things, but they don't give the algorithms for exactly how to do that thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such patents are sometimes easier to invalidate — in software contexts, failing to disclose algorithmic structure corresponding to claimed functions invites indefiniteness challenges. While drafters may use functional claiming to try to obtain broader patents, the lack of disclosed structure can make enforcement and validity more vulnerable in litigation.
